title: No slander
tomorrow: kiran texts simran: 'is everyone talking about me?' now what?

segments.voice: Yesterday, sweet speech, as Asa di Var asks. Being sweet to someone's face is the easy part. Today, the harder test: what gets said when they aren't in the room.
screen: `SWEET WORDS.` → `NOW, WHEN THEY'RE NOT IN THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Lunch, Tuesday. Simran's phone buzzes face-up on the table, then again, then it won't stop. The senior group chat has found a topic: Kiran. Kiran quit volleyball two weeks ago, stopped coming to lunch, leaves the second the bell rings. Someone types, she thinks she's too good for us now. Someone adds an old photo of hers, circled. Laughing faces stack up, and one of them is Simran's, sent before she thought. Now she has a joke ready, and it's a good one. Maya, beside her, says nothing. She just watches Simran's thumb. Simran types the joke. Her finger hovers over send.
screen: `THE GROUP CHAT FINDS A TOPIC.` → `ONE LAUGHING FACE IS SIMRAN'S.` → `HER FINGER HOVERS OVER SEND.`

segments.voice: There's a line from Guru Nanak, in a hymn in Raag Vadhans in the Guru Granth Sahib, that fits in a thumb's width. In paraphrase: don't call anyone bad; that only starts a quarrel. Then the turn. The quarrel isn't really with them. It's with the Master, and in that fight, the one who loses is the one who spoke. Sikh teaching has a word for talking people down behind their backs: ninda, slander. Notice what the line does not say. It doesn't say pretend nothing is ever wrong. It says don't call anyone bad: don't pass a sentence on someone in front of an audience. In Sohila, Guru Nanak says the same light is in everyone. A group chat is an audience that never goes home, and the person on trial isn't even there to hear it. Here's the part to tell a friend tonight: no slander usually starts small. Not a speech about kindness. Just the joke you don't send, the photo you don't add, one line that turns the chat a quarter inch. Simran deletes the joke. She types: has anyone just asked her? Nobody answers for a minute. Then a thumbs-up, and the chat moves on to prom.
screen: `GURU NANAK: DON'T CALL ANYONE BAD.` · `THE QUARREL IS WITH THE MASTER.` · `NINDA: TALKING PEOPLE DOWN.` · `THE JOKE YOU DON'T SEND.` · then, large: `NO GOSSIP.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind where talk about other people usually starts for you: a chat, a lunch table, a ride home. Name the moment it tips into mean, and one short sentence you could say instead. Then let the plan rest, and set your phone face down for the sit.
No slander. Not calling anyone bad behind their back, before an audience that can't be taken back. Ninda is slander.
Your line: no gossip. The joke you don't send still counts, even if nobody ever sees it. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1695 COUNTS.` → `LIVING IT · 69 OF 134.` → `TOMORROW: KIRAN ASKS: IS EVERYONE TALKING ABOUT ME?`

howItsDone: Sikh teaching treats ninda, slander, as a serious fault, and Sikhs are taught to steer talk away from putting people down, especially behind their backs.

pairs: is with the Master, not them

myth: gossip is fine as long as it's true
the line doesn't say 'unless it's true.' it says don't call anyone bad, don't pass sentence before an audience.
in Guru Nanak's line, the one who calls others bad is the one who loses
the quarrel is with the Master, and the speaker loses themself in it.

fork.reveal: the line says don't call anyone bad. even true details can become a sentence passed before an audience; asking her turns the talk back toward a person.

chat.meaning: The line warns against calling anyone bad. Venting can stay about her own feelings; the verdict on the roommate is the part to skip.
